name: Zane Ibrahim

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Zane. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so feel free to tell me what you'd say in public and also what you really think.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Sure, fire away. I'm Zane, I'm 27, and I work for a private home-care agency in the city that mostly looks after people who pay for themselves. I live with my partner Yasmin, who's a pharmacy technician.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I do longer visits, two or three hours, with five or so clients. Personal care, meals, taking someone to the barber, sometimes sitting with a person near the end of life while the district nurse comes and goes. I use AI every day, to plan my route, to write the weekly update to each family and to practise my Spanish for one client. What I like is the time with people. What wears me out is families who treat you like staff rather than someone who cares about their dad.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a bit of a letdown. I like the tools, so I'd hoped for more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AI was oversold but still useful, at least for the boring bits. With friends I'd say it's a good assistant and nothing more. Online I'd post the odd tip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's fine for me. Rich families will always pay for a person who turns up on time and remembers their mother takes two sugars. That market isn't going anywhere.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my clients and keep using AI for routes and updates. I'd start charging a bit on the side to set up tablets and video doorbells for clients' families, since I do it anyway for free. And I'd keep my savings ticking over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, a bit bored maybe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your Spanish practice. What else would you use AI for in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family updates, mostly. I tell the AI what happened in the visit and it writes a tidy summary for the son in Dubai or the daughter in another city. It saves me an hour a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you, even here?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. The agency is busy, and we've got about four months saved between us. Maybe my knees in twenty years.

think: I think **paying families** will always want a reliable person.

Keep our **four months** of savings ticking over.

He spots a **side income** in the tech help he already gives.

steps.text: Keep five private clients and AI route planning
Charge families for setting up tablets and video doorbells

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now that's interesting. The office side, booking and invoicing, goes to software. The actual caring stays with us for a while.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is good for carers who are willing to learn. At work I'd offer to show people the new tools. Online I'd probably start a little channel about tech for older people.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's mostly good for me. Every family I work for asks me how to set up the video doorbell, so I might as well charge for the know-how. The risk is the agency using software to squeeze our hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do a short course in home-tech installation in the spring, and register as self-employed for the side work. I'd spend about four hundred on a starter kit of sensors and tablets to show families. And I'd use every AI tool the agency brings in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, even a bit excited.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the agency change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Smaller office, same number of carers, maybe more clients because it's cheaper to run. The owner's quite sharp, she'd want to grow.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What about Yasmin's job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one worries me more. Checking prescriptions is exactly the thinking work that card mentions. She'd probably be fine for a few years, but we'd talk about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That's a punch. 2028 for thinking work, 2031 for my hands-on work. I'd be 32.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say publicly that carers need to get close to the robots now, not fight them. At work I'd push the owner to be first in the city to trial them properly. Online I'd be pretty loud about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Yasmin checks prescriptions at a pharmacy, so AI comes for her job in 2028 and for mine around 2031. We'd both need a new plan, fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd move into the care-tech side straight away, working for a company that installs home robots, or building my own setup business. I'd put three months of our savings into kit and training. And I'd push Yasmin to look at hands-on pharmacy work, like the clinic side.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, honestly, though I'd have a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Yasmin do in that gap between 2028 and 2031?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Build up our savings from Yasmin's last years at the pharmacy, and get my business going so it's earning by 2030. If the robots need setting up and supervising, someone local has to do it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you stay a carer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Part-time maybe, with my favourite clients. But mostly I'd be the person installing and checking the robots. I'd be sad about that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five and eight. That's a proper runway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to do it properly, with training and rules. At work I'd keep showing people tools. Online I'd say the same.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think it's a business opportunity. Eight years before the robots is enough to build a small business putting robots into old people's homes the right way. I'd have time to do it carefully.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep caring three days a week and spend two days building the setup business. I'd get a proper installer certificate within two years. And I'd invest in a van once the work is steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly keen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Like you said with the fast one, you'd move to care-tech. Does five years change that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. I'd just do it slower and keep caring longer. I'd rather keep my hands in the job while it's still human.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would worry you about running your own business?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The money side, getting paid on time, insurance. I've never run anything. Yasmin's better with paperwork than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, then thirteen for robots. I'd be 40. Plenty of time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is the good version, if people use the time. At work I'd be upbeat. Online I'd keep posting tech tips for older people and their families.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Thirteen years before the robots is plenty, and I'd rather be the man selling the robot than the man it replaces. I'd build slowly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep caring full-time for a few years. I'd grow the side business bit by bit and save part of what it earns. Around year five I'd decide whether to go full-time on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Pretty optimistic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is ten years too much time for someone like you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. I'd get bored waiting. But I'd use it to save properly, which I'm not great at.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want Yasmin to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Retrain early into something hands-on in health, maybe as a pharmacy clinic assistant. She'd have time, which she wouldn't with the fast one.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because Yasmin and I would both be hit within three years. What would help is cheap training for carers in care tech, and some rules so families can't just swap a person for a machine overnight. The robots will need someone who can talk to a frightened 90-year-old, and I plan to be that someone.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask about the families. They pay, so they decide. Some would buy a robot tomorrow to save money, and some would never let one in the house.

headlineQuote: The robots will need someone who can talk to a frightened 90-year-old, and I plan to be that someone.
portrait: Zane is a **27-year-old carer** at a private agency serving families who pay for themselves.
He lives with his partner Yasmin, a **pharmacy technician**, and they have about four months saved.
He uses **AI daily** and already helps families set up home tech for free.
He sees a **business** in installing and supervising care robots and would invest early.
He stays calm in slower pictures, but is **anxious** in AGI by 2028 because both jobs are hit.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, with both his and Yasmin's jobs hit within three years.
whatWouldHelp: **Cheap care-tech training** for carers, and rules against overnight swaps.
